title: Yunus, Hud and Yusuf
intro: 26 days through three Meccan surahs named after prophets, ending with the story of Yusuf told from beginning to end.

posts.caption: This plan reads three Meccan surahs named after prophets: Yunus (Jonah), Hud and Yusuf (Joseph). Surah Yunus, the tenth, has 109 verses. This verse pictures the people of Paradise: their prayer is to glorify Allah, their greeting is peace, and their last word is praise, in the words of Al-Fatiha's second verse. The words that open the Quran's first surah become the closing words of those in the Garden.

The point is that Allah's invitation is open to all: He calls everyone to Dar as-Salam, "the abode of peace", a name for Paradise, while guiding to a straight path whom He wills. As-Salam, "the Peace", is also one of the names of Allah (59:23), so some commentators read it as the home of the One who is Peace. Just before, worldly life is compared to a crop that flourishes and is suddenly gone.

This comes after verses about people who hear the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ without really listening. It states a principle the Quran returns to often: Allah does no injustice to anyone, and people wrong only their own souls. "Aught" is Pickthall's old word for "anything".

Addressed to all people, this verse describes the Quran four ways: an exhortation, a healing for the heart, a guidance and a mercy. "Balm" translates shifa, healing, and "that which is in the breasts" is an Arabic way of saying the inner self. Muslims often quote it when they speak of the Quran as a comfort.

posts.display: Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve. Those who believe and keep their duty (to Allah).
posts.caption: "Friends of Allah" translates awliya (singular wali), those who are close to Him and under His protection. The point lies in the second verse, which defines them simply as people who believe and have taqwa, a mindful awareness of Allah; Ibn Kathir draws from it that every believer mindful of Allah is His friend. "No fear and no grief" is a promise the Quran makes to the faithful many times.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) speaks to the few among his people who believed in him, though they feared Pharaoh. He asks them for tawakkul, trust in Allah that leaves the outcome in His hands. "Surrendered" renders muslimin, those who submit to Allah. In the next verse they answer: "In Allah we put trust."

Just before this, verse 98 recalls the people of the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), the one town that believed in time to be spared. Then the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reminded that faith cannot be forced on anyone. It echoes "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256).

Surah Hud, the eleventh, is Meccan and has 123 verses. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi's collection reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said Hud and similar surahs had turned his hair grey, a remark often linked to their sobering warnings. This verse is gentler, and its point is reassurance: every creature's provision, rizq, rests with Allah, who knows its dwelling and its final resting place.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah) boards the ship as the flood begins, calling on the name of Allah for its sailing and its anchoring. The point is trust at the moment of greatest danger: he places the whole voyage in Allah's hands. "Its course and its mooring" translates majraha wa mursaha. Some Muslims recite this line when they set out by boat or begin a journey.

The Prophet Hud, after whom the surah is named, was sent to 'Ad, an ancient Arabian people the Quran describes as powerful builders. Rejected and mocked by them, he answers with tawakkul, trust in Allah. Holding a creature "by the forelock" is an Arabic image of complete control: nothing moves outside Allah's power.

Angels come to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in human form. He returns their greeting of peace and hurries to serve them a roasted calf, and his hospitality is often held up as a model in Islamic tradition. They bring good news: a son, Ishaq (Isaac), born to him and his wife in their old age.

The Prophet Shu'ayb (Pickthall spells it Shu'eyb) was sent to Midian, a trading people he urged to give honest weight and measure. Even while warning them, he holds the door open: ask forgiveness and turn back, for Allah is merciful and loving. His appeal uses a rare divine name, al-Wadud, "the Loving", which appears in the Quran only here and in Surah Al-Buruj (85:14).

Commentators connect the times named here, the two ends of the day and the early hours of the night, with the daily prayers. "Establish worship" is Pickthall's rendering of keeping up the prayer, salah. The second half is one of the Quran's most hopeful lines: good deeds wipe away bad ones.

Surah Hud tells of Nuh (Noah), Hud, Salih, Ibrahim (Abraham), Lut (Lot), Shu'ayb and Musa (Moses). Near its end it explains why: to make firm the heart of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through years of opposition in Mecca. The next surah, Yusuf, is one long story of its own.

Surah Yusuf, the twelfth, is Meccan and has 111 verses. Unusually, it tells one prophet's story as a single, continuous narrative. Many readers take "the best of narratives" (ahsan al-qasas) to mean the story that follows; some commentators apply it to all the Quran's stories. "Heedless" here means unaware: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had not known these stories before they were revealed.

The story begins with a dream. The young Yusuf (Joseph) tells his father, the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob), that he saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. Pickthall's "planets" translates kawkab, a star or planet. What the dream means becomes clear only near the end of the story.

The Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) sees in the dream a sign that Allah has chosen Yusuf (Joseph), and he fears the jealousy of his other sons. "O my dear son" renders ya bunayya, a tender form of address. His fear proves right: resentful of their father's love for Yusuf, the older brothers take him away and throw him into a well.

The brothers bring back the shirt of Yusuf (Joseph) stained with false blood, claiming a wolf ate him. The Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) does not believe them. His answer is sabrun jamil, "comely patience", often explained as patience without complaint to people, turning to Allah alone for help.

A passing caravan pulls Yusuf (Joseph) out of the well and sells him in Egypt, where a high official, called al-'Aziz in the surah, takes him into his household. There, far from home, he grows up and Allah gives him wisdom and knowledge. The point is that Allah's care follows him through every reversal, and rewards those who do good, al-muhsinin.

The official's wife tries to seduce Yusuf (Joseph). When he refuses, she and other women of the city press him, and he is threatened with prison. He prays that prison is dearer to him than giving in. Allah turns their schemes away from him, and he is jailed for a time though innocent.

In prison, Yusuf (Joseph) explains the dreams of two fellow prisoners and speaks to them of the One God. The one who is freed forgets to mention him, and he stays in prison for some years. Then the king of Egypt has a dream his courtiers cannot read, and it becomes the turning point that will bring Yusuf out. "Kine" is an old word for cows.

Yusuf (Joseph) reads the king's dream as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, and advises storing grain. Cleared of the old accusation, he is put in charge of the storehouses of Egypt. When famine spreads, his brothers come to buy grain from the brother they threw into the well.

Yusuf (Joseph) has kept his younger brother in Egypt by a ruse, and their father, the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob), weeps until his eyes turn white. Told he will grieve himself to death, he answers with this line. The point is where he takes his sorrow: not to people, but to Allah alone, whom he still trusts. In the next verse he sends his sons back to search, telling them never to despair of Allah's mercy.

On their third visit, Yusuf (Joseph) tells his brothers who he is, and they admit their wrong. "Have no fear" renders la tathrib, "no reproach". According to accounts in the sira, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ quoted these words in 630 CE, when he entered Mecca and pardoned the people who had driven him out.

Yusuf (Joseph) sends his shirt home; laid on his father's face, it restores his sight. The whole family comes to Egypt, and Yusuf welcomes his parents. In the next verse they bow before him in honour, and he says this is the meaning of his dream of old: the eleven stars, the sun and the moon.

Surah Yusuf ends where it began, with the worth of these stories: a lesson for people of understanding, a guidance and a mercy. That closes this walk through Yunus, Hud and Yusuf, from the abode of peace to a family made whole again. Thank you for reading along.
